script.text: Good morning! I'm Kelly, and this is your daily lesson for February 26. Today we're exploring two powerful ideas together.
A lake seems eternal—sitting there, still and permanent.  But lakes are geological newcomers.  Most are younger than human civilization.

Most lakes in temperate regions were carved by glaciers during the last ice age—only 15,000 years ago. Massive ice sheets gouged depressions, then melted and filled them. The Great Lakes are glacier footprints filled with their own melted ice. Lake Baikal in Siberia is the oldest and deepest lake on Earth—25 million years old and 5,387 feet deep.  It holds 20% of the world's unfrozen freshwater.

Today's wisdom: Here's today's wisdom: What seems permanent is often just slow.  Lakes remind us that stillness is temporary, that all containers eventually fill, and that what looks eternal is just changing at a pace we can't perceive.
Now let's take what we learned and put it into practice.
Today's growth challenge is Temporary Treasures - Value What Won't Last.

Here's your activity: Identify something in your life that seems permanent but is actually slowly changing—a relationship stage, a life phase, a situation. Acknowledge its impermanence. Does knowing it won't last forever change how you experience it today? This helps you appreciate things precisely because they're temporary.
And here's how today's lessons connect: What you learned about where lakes come from can be applied to temporary treasures - value what won't last. Practice makes progress.
That's today's lesson. Learn something, grow a little. I'll see you tomorrow with something new. Stay curious!
